title: Dealing with Contention System Design Quiz

questions.question: What does the SQL 'FOR UPDATE' clause accomplish?
questions.explanation: FOR UPDATE acquires an exclusive lock on the selected rows, preventing other transactions from accessing them until the transaction completes. This is what lets you read rows, decide in application code (like finding an open block of adjacent seats), and write before letting go.
options: It updates many rows at once in a single atomic batch operation
It acquires an exclusive lock on the rows the SELECT returns
It automatically retries any update statements that happen to fail
It creates a backup copy of the affected rows before updating

questions.question: Optimistic concurrency control performs better than pessimistic locking when conflicts are frequent.
questions.explanation: Optimistic concurrency control works best when conflicts are rare - frequent conflicts mean lots of retries, making pessimistic locking more efficient.

questions.question: You reuse a restaurant's review_count as your optimistic-concurrency version. Between your read and write, one review is deleted and another is added, so the count returns to its original value. Your write succeeds but silently clobbers the change in between. What is this called?
questions.explanation: The ABA problem occurs when a value changes from A to B and back to A between your read and write. An equality check can't see the round trip. The safe fix is a dedicated version column that increments on every update regardless of whether any business data changed. Only reuse a business value when it moves in one direction, like an ever-increasing bid.
options: A deadlock, where each transaction waits on the other forever
The ABA problem, where a value changes and returns to its original
Write skew, where two valid decisions together break an invariant
A lost update from a single missed read-modify-write cycle

questions.question: Which approach works best for handling write contention on a 'hot partition' where many users want to modify the same resource simultaneously?
questions.explanation: When contention lands on one specific row, normal scaling breaks down: sharding can't split a single row, load balancers just queue requests on that same row, and read replicas don't touch writes. Queue-based serialization funnels all requests for that resource through a single worker, eliminating contention by making operations sequential. The tradeoff is capped throughput and a single point of failure to back with a standby.
options: Add more database shards to spread the write load horizontally
Route reads to a pool of read replicas to take load off the primary
Queue-based serialization through a single worker
Increase server capacity so the requests are processed faster

questions.question: When should you choose pessimistic locking over optimistic concurrency control?
questions.explanation: Pessimistic locking provides predictable performance and handles high contention better. When collisions are common, locking upfront beats optimistic concurrency, where constant retries cost more than the lock ever did.
options: When conflicts are rare and the occasional retry is cheap for the app
When you simply need the best possible raw performance
When conflicts are frequent and constant retries would be costly
When the system happens to be distributed across several nodes

questions.question: Two users try to buy the last concert ticket at the same time. Both see '1 ticket available' and both proceed to purchase. What is the root cause of this double-booking?
questions.explanation: This is a lost update, the classic failure of a read-modify-write cycle. Both users read '1 seat available' before either commits their update, so both proceed thinking the seat is available. The fix is to close the gap between reading a value and acting on it.
options: Both read the same count before either commits, so each thinks a ticket is left
The database briefly lost connectivity and dropped one of the purchase requests
The server lacked the capacity to handle both purchase requests at once
Network latency between the users and the server delayed one of the writes

questions.question: A purchase transaction first runs a conditional decrement on `available_seats`, then unconditionally inserts a ticket row. Under contention, the decrement sometimes matches zero rows, but the ticket insert still commits. What is the correct fix?
questions.explanation: An `UPDATE` that matches zero rows is not automatically an error; it can succeed while doing nothing. The ticket creation must be conditional on the reservation update succeeding, otherwise a user can get a ticket without actually reserving capacity.
options: Treat the zero-row update as a successful reservation because the transaction committed.
Make the insert depend on the update actually changing a row, such as using `UPDATE ... RETURNING` or checking affected row count.
Move the insert before the decrement so the ticket exists before capacity is checked.
Remove the transaction because the conditional update is already atomic.

questions.question: A booking system runs `UPDATE concerts SET available_seats = available_seats - 1 WHERE concert_id = 'weeknd_tour' AND available_seats > 0`. Why is this safe under concurrency without any explicit lock?
questions.explanation: When the check is a predicate on the row you're writing, the database evaluates it and makes the change in a single atomic statement. The database serializes writes to the same row, so the second update re-checks `available_seats > 0` against the row the first one left behind, finds it false, and changes nothing. The check and the decrement are one step, so there's no gap to slip into.
options: The application reads the seat count and checks it in code before sending the UPDATE
The database serializes same-row writes, so the loser re-checks the condition and changes nothing
SELECT statements are guaranteed to run before any UPDATE on the same connection
The WHERE clause automatically takes out an exclusive lock across the entire concerts table for you

questions.question: A concert has 20 seats left. Alice and Bob both select seat A15, and each transaction only checks `available_seats > 0` before inserting a ticket for A15. The seat count remains valid, but A15 is double-sold. What design change addresses the real contention?
questions.explanation: The counter only protects the question “is there any ticket left,” not “is this exact seat available.” To prevent double-selling A15, the conditional write must target the contended resource itself: the individual seat or ticket row.
options: Increase the seat counter by one before each purchase attempt.
Use a stricter timestamp format for ticket purchase times.
Guard the specific seat row with a conditional update like `status = 'available'`.
Store the seat count in a cache instead of the database.

questions.question: What is the standard solution for preventing deadlocks with pessimistic locking?
questions.explanation: Ordered locking prevents deadlocks by breaking the circular wait condition. Sort all the resources you need by a deterministic key (like primary key) and always acquire them in that order, regardless of your business logic flow. This way two transactions touching the same rows can't each hold one lock while waiting on the other.
options: Switch to optimistic concurrency instead of using pessimistic locking
Always acquire your locks in a consistent, globally sorted order
Set shorter lock-wait timeouts on every transaction that locks rows
Run every transaction at the SERIALIZABLE isolation level instead

questions.question: For group bookings, the app runs `SELECT ... FOR UPDATE` over every available seat in the floor section, spends 200 ms finding four adjacent seats, updates them, and commits. If all requests target that same section and no `SKIP LOCKED`-style behavior is used, what is the approximate maximum throughput caused by this locking strategy?
questions.explanation: The article’s `FOR UPDATE` example locks all open seats in the section while the app decides, so competing group bookings wait rather than proceed independently. A 200 ms critical section gives an upper bound of roughly `1 / 0.2 = 5` serialized bookings per second for that section.
options: About 250 bookings/second, because each booking only sells 4 seats and the section has many rows.
About 50 bookings/second, because 50 concurrent clients can all hold shared read locks while scanning.
Unbounded until the database CPU is saturated, because row locks only block updates, not reads.
About 5 bookings/second, because the transactions effectively serialize while holding the same locked seat set for 200 ms each.

questions.question: Two on-call engineers each independently confirm the other is still on call, then both step down at the same moment, leaving nobody on call. They wrote to different rows, so a row lock, a version check, and a conditional WHERE all sailed through. What is this conflict, and what catches it?
questions.explanation: This is write skew. Each transaction reads an overlapping set of rows, makes a decision that's valid on its own, and only together do they break an invariant. Because no single row collides, the per-row tools miss it. SERIALIZABLE makes the database track these read-write dependencies and aborts one transaction. Often cheaper still is to materialize the invariant onto a single row (a count on the team row, or a FOR UPDATE on it) so the simpler tools can guard it.
options: A deadlock, prevented by always acquiring all of your locks in one consistent global order
Write skew, caught by SERIALIZABLE or a single-row materialized invariant
The ABA problem, caught by a dedicated incrementing version column
A lost update, caught by one conditional write with the right WHERE

questions.question: A purchase transaction runs a conditional decrement and then unconditionally inserts a ticket: `UPDATE concerts SET available_seats = available_seats - 1 WHERE concert_id = ? AND available_seats > 0; INSERT INTO tickets ...; COMMIT;`. During a sellout, some transactions create tickets even though they did not get a seat. What is the precise bug?
questions.explanation: Transactions make the decrement and insert commit or roll back together, but they do not automatically turn a zero-row update into a failure. The article’s fix is to make the insert consume the `UPDATE ... RETURNING` result, or check the affected row count and roll back when it is zero.
options: The transaction is missing `FOR UPDATE`, so the database can interleave the two statements inside a single transaction.
An `UPDATE` that matches zero rows is a successful no-op, so the later `INSERT` still commits unless the app checks affected rows or makes the insert depend on `RETURNING`.
The database applies the `INSERT` before the `UPDATE` at commit time, so the ticket can be visible before the seat is reserved.
The conditional `WHERE available_seats > 0` is evaluated only once when the transaction begins, so it cannot see concurrent commits.

questions.question: A checkout flow holds seat A15 with Redis `SET seat:A15 alice NX EX 600`. Alice's server hits a GC pause that outlasts the 600-second TTL, Bob's server then runs the same command for A15, and Alice's server resumes. What is true of this design?
questions.explanation: A TTL lock expires on the clock, not when the holder is finished. Once Alice's key lapses, `SET NX` lets Bob take it, and Alice's resumed server has no way to know it lost the lock. For a seat hold that's a rare, harmless hiccup, but the final sale should still be enforced at the source of truth, such as a conditional write on the seat row.
options: Bob's `SET` fails, because `NX` keeps a key alive for as long as the client that created it is still connected to the Redis server.
Bob's `SET` overwrites Alice's key, and Redis then rejects any further writes for seat A15 that arrive from Alice's server.
Both servers briefly think they hold A15, so a plain TTL lock is fine for a soft hold but not where a double grant corrupts data.
Alice's hold is extended automatically, because Redis restarts a key's TTL when its owner resumes after the pause.

questions.question: Two buyers concurrently run `UPDATE concerts SET available_seats = available_seats - 1 WHERE available_seats > 0` under `SERIALIZABLE` isolation, and the loser's transaction aborts with a serialization error. Because that error does not reveal whether any seats remain, the application should retry the transaction rather than tell the buyer the concert is sold out.
questions.explanation: A serialization error only means the transaction conflicted with a concurrent writer; the winner may have taken seat 7 of 100, leaving plenty for the loser. Retrying re-runs the decrement against the committed state, so it either succeeds or matches zero rows, and only that zero-row result means the concert is sold out. At common defaults like `READ COMMITTED`, the loser skips the error and re-checks the predicate directly, which is why the article says only the failure shape changes.
